query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A machine‐learning enhanced atomistic simulation that explicitly incorporates defect scattering and 1 wt.% oxygen impurities in bulk HfNbTaTiZr will predict temperature‐dependent electrical conductivity in both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes with significantly improved accuracy compared to analytical models based on perfect crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr high-entropy alloy synthesized with an intrinsic population of point defects and a controlled 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Implement a ML-enhanced atomistic simulation that explicitly includes scattering from point defects and oxygen impurities.
generation.conditions: Temperature regimes at 0–200 K (low temperature) and 300–1200 K (high temperature) on specimens matching the above material state.
generation.structural_mediator: Defects (including oxygen interstitials) modify local bonding and electronic structure, leading to additional scattering events that influence charge transport.
generation.mechanism: The simulation framework predicts conductivity by statistically sampling defect configurations and their impact on electron scattering, thus capturing the interplay between thermal activation and impurity/defect scattering, which is neglected in traditional perfect-crystal analytical models.
generation.predicted_outcome: Simulated conductivity values should align closely with experimental measurements across both temperature ranges, with relative errors significantly lower than those of idealized, defect-free models (e.g., within an acceptable deviation threshold, potentially less than 20% error compared to experimental benchmarks).
generation.baseline: Conventional analytical predictions that assume a pristine, defect‐free crystal structure which typically show larger discrepancies from experimental data due to neglect of defect and oxygen impurity scattering.
generation.boundary: The approach is expected to be valid only for HfNbTaTiZr alloys with similar defect populations and around 1 wt.% oxygen; predictions may not extend to purer or more highly oxidized samples or to temperature regimes outside 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements and the precise error margins remain uncertain until further calibration against a comprehensive set of experimental conductivity data.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with 1 wt.% oxygen and quantify their conductivity in two key temperature windows (near 150 K and 800 K). Run the ML-enhanced atomistic simulations incorporating the measured defect and oxygen levels to predict conductivity. Compare the predictions with the experimental measurements.
measurements: Electrical conductivity at ~150 K measured using low-temperature transport measurements.
Electrical conductivity at ~800 K measured using high-temperature conductivity apparatus.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experimental conductivity values deviate from the simulation predictions by more than a pre-established threshold (e.g., 20% relative error) in either temperature regime, then the hypothesis that the ML-enhanced approach significantly improves prediction accuracy would be falsified.

Options for sustainable clean energy include advanced power generation systems that have the potential to drastically reduce the emission of greenhouse gases. These advanced systems are often required to operate under harsh conditions to optimize efficiency, which poses several challenges for the available materials. An example of advanced power system is one that is associated with fusion energy [1] . Beyond traditional fission-based systems, fusion reactors not only promise nearly unlimited clean energy, but also avoid the generation of long-life radioactive waste produced in fission devices. One remaining challenge is that of materials, which can withstand extreme conditions of radiation, temperature, and stress, with long-term steady properties for the power plant to be economically viable [2] – [4] . Alloy samples were repeatedly melted at least 10 times to ensure uniform melting and improve their chemical homogeneity. After cooling, the bulk ingots with dimensions of 50 mm × 50 mm × 10 mm were homogenized at 1200 °C for 5 h in an Ar atmosphere and subsequently hot-rolled at 1200 °C with a rolling reduction ratio of 80%, i.e., with a thickness reduction from 10 to 2 mm. After hot rolling, the ingots were rolled at ambient temperature (25 °C) with a reduction ratio of 75% to reduce the thickness from 2 to 0.5 mm (this is termed the cold-rolled alloy). Metallic alloys containing multiple principal alloying elements, which are known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [1] – [3] , have attracted extensive research interest in recent years with many studies focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and underlying deformation mechanisms [4] – [6] . For example, as a new class of structural materials, certain face-centered cubic ( fcc ) alloys, in particular CrCoNi-based HEAs, have been shown to possess improved strength and exceptional damage tolerance, especially at cryogenic temperatures [7] , [8] .

decision.trend: Earlier analytical models for high‐entropy alloys like HfNbTaTiZr assumed perfect, defect‐free crystals, so they could only capture limited aspects of temperature-dependent transport properties. Subsequent experimental and simulation studies—such as those exploring processing routes, oxygen uptake, and microstructural control in bulk HfNbTaTiZr—have demonstrated that even small oxygen contents (around 1 wt.%) and processing-induced defects can strongly affect material properties. However, these studies have mostly focused on microstructure and mechanical strength rather than on electron transport. The field has thus moved from idealized treatments toward incorporating real-world defect and impurity effects, although accurate conductivity predictions over both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes still remain unsolved.
decision.unsolved: No existing method integrates explicit defect and oxygen impurity effects into a single predictive framework for electrical conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr across both the low temperature (0–200 K) and high temperature (300–1200 K) ranges. The challenge is to overcome the inaccuracy introduced by idealized models and to establish a calibrated simulation that matches the benchmark conductivity measured on specimens with 1 wt.% oxygen.
decision.lever: explicit inclusion of defect and impurity effects using machine‐learning enhanced atomistic simulation
decision.why: Building on the observed trend—where initial models using perfect crystals were later supplemented by studies quantifying oxygen and defect effects in bulk HfNbTaTiZr—the most plausible next step is to develop a predictive computational framework that leverages machine learning to incorporate scattering from point defects and 1 wt.% oxygen. This approach will enable calculation of temperature‐dependent conductivity over both the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes and directly address the identified performance and method limitations. A held-out benchmark might be a measured conductivity value (e.g., a deviation beyond a specified threshold at 150 K) that would falsify the hypothesis if the predicted impact of defects does not align with experimental observations.
